title: The Convenient Format

scenario.situation: The analytics engineering team has standardized every dataset on a proprietary warehouse-native format because benchmarks show it queries 30–40% faster than alternatives.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead architect assumes that because the format wins on query speed inside the warehouse, it is the right default for all datasets company-wide.
scenario.question: Is fastest-here really the right criterion for choosing a storage standard?

decisions.prompt: The lead wants you to validate the format choice. How do you frame the investigation?

options.label: Reproduce the benchmark
options.detail: Re-run the query-speed benchmarks yourself to confirm or challenge the 30–40% claim.
options.consequence: You confirm the benchmark is accurate. The format is indeed faster inside the warehouse — but you've only answered the question that was already answered, and haven't touched whether speed is the right criterion.
options.divergenceCost: Anchored entirely on the lead's criterion and validated the assumption rather than interrogating it.

options.label: Counterfactual access audit
options.detail: Map every current and roadmap use case against the format: which engines, pipelines, and teams can actually read it, and what does switching cost later?
options.consequence: You immediately surface that several roadmap workloads — a new Spark-based ML pipeline, a partner data-share, and a planned migration — cannot read the proprietary format at all. Speed inside one engine is only part of the picture.

options.label: Cost analysis of storage
options.detail: Compare raw storage costs for the proprietary format versus open alternatives.
options.consequence: Storage costs turn out nearly equivalent. You've produced a true but irrelevant finding — the real risk isn't the bill, it's whether the data is accessible at all.
options.divergenceCost: Optimized for the wrong dimension and left the lock-in risk entirely invisible.

options.label: Vendor best-practice review
options.detail: Check the warehouse vendor's own documentation for recommended format usage.
options.consequence: Unsurprisingly, the vendor recommends its own format. This is circular — the vendor's incentive is retention, not your portability. You've outsourced the framing to the most biased source.
options.divergenceCost: Deferred the framing to a conflicted source and introduced vendor bias into the investigation.

decisions.prompt: The access audit surfaces a range of datasets. Which metric do you use to evaluate the format decision across them?

artifact.title: Query speed improvement vs. open formats — by dataset (seconds saved per query)
artifact.caption: Raw seconds saved by using the proprietary format. Looks uniformly positive — but does speed matter equally for every use case?

options.label: Query speed delta (seconds saved) per dataset
options.detail: Rank datasets by how much faster the proprietary format is.
options.consequence: Every dataset shows some speed gain, so the format looks like a universal win. But you're measuring only the benefit and not the cost — engine compatibility and migration risk are completely off the chart.
options.divergenceCost: Measured only the upside of one criterion, making an asymmetric trade-off invisible.

options.label: Portability-weighted access score per dataset
options.detail: For each dataset, combine: (1) speed gain, (2) number of engines/tools that can read it natively, and (3) estimated switching cost if the format must change later.
options.consequence: Normalized across all three dimensions, the picture flips: dashboard aggregates justify the proprietary format, but the ML feature store, partner share, and archive datasets score far better on open formats — the switching-cost penalty overwhelms the speed gain for anything that must leave the warehouse.

artifact.title: Portability-weighted access score by dataset (higher = open format wins)
artifact.caption: Negative = proprietary format wins; positive = open format wins after weighting speed, engine compatibility, and switching cost. Three of five dataset classes favor open formats decisively.

decisions.prompt: The weighted analysis shows open formats win for most roadmap-critical datasets. What do you tell the lead architect?

options.label: "The proprietary format is the wrong choice — migrate everything to Parquet/Iceberg now."
options.detail: Make the full causal call and recommend an immediate blanket migration.
options.consequence: You've overcorrected: the proprietary format genuinely is optimal for pure-warehouse workloads like dashboard aggregates. A blanket migration would degrade those with no benefit, and you've presented a correlation-based scoring model as a certainty.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed the analysis as definitive and recommended a blanket action that ignores legitimate use cases.

options.label: "Speed isn't the only criterion — portability scores suggest open formats for roadmap-critical datasets, but let's pilot on one before setting a new standard."
options.detail: Present the finding, flag the scoring model's assumptions, and recommend a bounded pilot to validate.
options.consequence: You reframe the decision from 'which format is fastest?' to 'which format fits each workload?' The lead sees that the current standard optimizes for a real but narrow criterion. A pilot on the ML feature store will surface real switching costs before the team commits to a new standard.

insight: The proprietary format's speed advantage is real but local — it only holds inside a single engine. When roadmap workloads require Spark, external partners, or future portability, the switching cost dwarfs the query-time savings. The lesson is that foundational storage decisions must be evaluated on a multi-dimensional scorecard — speed, engine reach, and lock-in cost — not on the benchmark that was convenient to run. A sound architect doesn't challenge the measurement; they challenge whether the right thing was measured.
